I thank the distinguished representative of New Zealand, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Canada.

Senator Hawley. Madam President, yesterday my wife and I had the opportunity and the great honor of attending a service in this building, a memorial service that was held to commemorate the courage, the suffering of those who died and were injured in the terrible Hamas attack on Israel and innocent civilians on October 7th, 2 years ago, and at the same time to reflect on the courage and the extraordinary heroism of women who were involved in saving lives. And it's important for us to remember that the attack that took place on that day was the most dramatic attack on Israel and on Jewish citizens that had taken place since the Holocaust. We need to be able to hold in our hearts and in our minds 2 thoughts at the same time. The first is to understand the depth of the trauma that has been felt by the Israeli people because of the nature of that attack, and also their feeling that the rest of the world was indifferent or not sufficiently responding to the nature of that assault. Canada continues to condemn unequivocally Hamas's brutal terrorist attacks on October 7th, 2023, and we call once again for the immediate release of all the remaining hostages. And so we need to retain in our minds that sense. But we also need to recognize the sheer horror of the catastrophe that has taken place in Gaza. I do not intend to use this podium to, in any way, take away from what I've said earlier about the nature of the attack that took place on October 7th. But just as we recognize that, we also have to recognize the nature of the attacks that took place in response to the original attack. Canada believes that, yes, there's a right to self-defense. But there's also an obligation to carry out self-defense in a way that creates the least damage possible to human life. And that's not just some personal view, that happens to be the law. That's what the law tells us we have to do. We now see that famine is spreading, essential services have collapsed, Medical infrastructure is decimated, and humanitarian access remains severely obstructed in Gaza. This is further exacerbated by the repeated displacement of a vulnerable population. We see the pictures constantly of people moving around in the hundreds of thousands. The scale of human suffering is intolerable and demands urgent and collective action. And so, as we call for the immediate release of all the remaining hostages, we also repeat our call once again for an immediate and permanent ceasefire to protect civilians, including humanitarian workers. The level of aid that is now reaching civilians in Gaza is not acceptable. It does not meet the standards of common decency. And it does not meet the standards of international humanitarian law. Israel has an obligation to allow and facilitate the rapid and unimpeded passage of humanitarian aid in accordance with this law. This includes reopening all crossings and corridors, allowing the entry of essential supplies, including food, water, shelter, fuel, and medicine, Allowing the UN, including UNRWA, the Red Cross, and experienced humanitarian NGO partners to operate freely and safely across Gaza. The efforts that have been made by Israel and by others to establish some kind of an alternative to this reasoned, necessary approach do not meet the standard. They do not meet the test. They have not been a success. And we need to understand that. We have to have impartial, needs-based humanitarian assistance that is free from political interference of any kind. Aid must reach all citizens throughout the entirety of the Gaza Strip. Canada regrets that this resolution was blocked by a veto. And that's why we agreed on the need for this debate, and we will have further discussions on the need for United Nations reform. But we also want to make it clear, as our Prime Minister has stated yesterday, that we welcome the efforts that have been led by the United States and by President Trump that were announced. on September 29th to bring an end to the devastating war in Gaza and to secure the release of all hostages. We must seize the current momentum to lay the foundation for lasting peace through credible post-war security and governance arrangements in Gaza. Canada also joined with our French colleagues and our Saudi colleagues and many others to sign the New York Declaration and also to recognize the need for a sovereign Palestine and to recognize the State of Palestine, which we did. We have to advance towards a two-state solution, which we continue to believe is the only viable path to long-term peace and security for Israelis, for Palestinians and the Middle East more broadly. Nearly 2 years after the atrocities of October 7th, we must work to ensure that they are never allowed to be repeated, and we will stand by to support these efforts. For further clarity, let me repeat once more: To Hamas, we say, The war should be over. You have an obligation to free the hostages. Your seizing of the hostages was a crime of war. Your holding of the hostages is an ongoing crime of war. You must release the hostages. You must lay down your arms. The war must stop. Hamas needs to accept the need for peace. And that they, because of what they've done, they can have no role in the future governance of the State of Palestine. To Israel, we say quite simply, do everything you can to accept the responsibility of following the basic standards of international law. 2 states must be allowed. We have to get to a point where we see the logic of accepting the reality of the other. It will not do to focus only on our own suffering and fail to recognize the suffering of other people. And to all of us, I have to say we have watched with admiration the efforts of so many to lead us in a better direction. To my French and To our Saudi colleagues, I say we are in your debt for having refused to accept the view that there's nothing more to be done, and in fact to insist that the two states has to be brought back. To our American friends, we say, yes, well done on what is an extraordinary effort to bring together many countries from the region that in the past were never have taken this leap and never have gone this far. We all have a job, but we say this— I don't see these 2 efforts as being contradictory or one against the other. We don't have to pick sides. We have to pick the side of peace. We have to pick the side of dignity. We have to pick the side of reconciliation. of reconstruction, of renewal. This is the side we have to pick, and this is the side that my country has chosen. We believe profoundly that both Palestinians and Israelis have the same rights to peace, have the same rights to security, have the same rights to sovereignty, and have the same rights to prosperity. And we all have an ongoing obligation to make sure that we take the path forward. Sometimes people say these debates don't matter, that the words are empty. I often hear people stand up in this podium and say words don't matter, and they proceed to give further words. That's human nature. I often hear politicians stand at a podium and say, I'm not a politician. as soon as you stand at the podium, you are. You have to understand, we are all in this together. This debate is helpful in allowing us to focus on the enormity of the moment and the challenge that we face together, and that's what we have to live up to. Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you all. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Canada, and I now give the I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil.

Mr.

President, dear colleagues, it's always a challenge to speak right after Ambassador Bob Rae, one of our greatest orators in our General Assembly. Madam President, Brazil deeply regrets that on September 18th, the Security Council, on its symbolic 10,000th meeting, once again failed to meet its responsibilities under the UN Charter. 14 members voted in favor of a resolution that could have offered a concrete step toward alleviating the suffering in Gaza, yet the will of the international community was blocked again by the veto. The repeated and excessive resort to the veto has become a systemic failure of the Council. Instead of preserving peace and security, it has too often obstructed collective action, prevented responses to egregious violations of international humanitarian and human rights law, and perpetuated cycles of violence. The cost is measured not in abstractions, but in human lives, including children, women and humanitarian workers. Nowhere is this clearer than in Gaza, where we are witnessing one of the gravest humanitarian crises of our time. The destruction, deprivation and suffering inflicted on civilians constitute a collective tragedy. Brazil has consistently condemned these atrocities and all violations of international humanitarian law, including the taking of hostages. The Council must uphold its responsibilities under the UN Charter and in respect of our common humanity. Continued paralysis in the face of what the international community has already recognized as genocide is indefensible. Despite repeated briefings, consultations, and draft resolutions, the Council has been unable to take the decisive measures required. This paralysis undermines its credibility and erodes the foundations of multilateralism. Brazil calls for a profound reflection on the veto. It must never be a shield for impunity or a tool perpetuate suffering. The credibility of the Council depends on its ability to act. Inaction is costing thousands of innocent lives in Gaza and beyond. It is time for the Council to live up to its Charter responsibilities. The world cannot wait anymore. Gaza cannot wait anymore. Civilians martyred by conflict everywhere cannot wait anymore. Enough is enough. Lastly, we also regret that Resolution 76/262 has fallen short of the expectations to inhibit Council members to cast vetoes. Coming to the GA to explain the reasons why a resolution was vetoed has simply become naturalized. It has become nothing more than a platform for permanent members to voice before the entire General Assembly the same arguments they used to block Council action.

Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Brazil, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Chile.

Thank you, Madam President. I take the floor before this General Assembly with a profound sense of responsibility. The responsibility of my country. I also take the floor with the conviction that our collective work as member states cannot be paralyzed in the face of human suffering. Once again, we are witnessing how the Security Council, an organ whose primary responsibility is to maintain international peace and security, how such an organ has remained silent as a result of a veto being cast. This inaction is something we've also seen previously. It was seen on the 4th of June this year and has served to prolong the suffering of thousands of civilians, including older persons, women, and children. For 2 years now, these people have seen much more than their lives and hope being snuffed out. In other words, the actions of the Security Council have a direct impact, a direct specific impact in terms of wreaking suffering upon women, children, and older persons, among others. In recent weeks, we have seen how through manifold initiatives the international community has not remained indifferent to the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. This emergency meeting, this very meeting, is a reflection of the will of all citizens who hope to see the United Nations remain faithful to its founding promise, that is, to protect the peace and security of succeeding generations. The General Assembly has the mandate and the moral obligation to act when the Security Council cannot do just that. Today, more than ever before, this principle must guide our collective action. It is for this reason that today we raise our voice loud and clear, and we will never tire of doing just that. We are speaking out to reaffirm basic principles enshrined in international law and international humanitarian law, principles regarding the urgent need for a ceasefire and to protect civilians. We wish to echo the appeal issued in the resolution presented by the Security Council, an appeal to engage in a political process that will lead to a just, lasting, and definitive solution based on the two-state solution With Israel and Palestine living in peace and security in accordance with resolutions adopted by the United Nations. Madam President, the trust and the, the confidence in and credibility of this organization depends on our ability to act on behalf of those who cannot speak out. For this reason, we are grateful to all of those that voted in favor of the resolution. That resolution has the protection of human life at its heart, as well as the imperative need for peace. Chile values and is hopeful in view of the mediation efforts and the peace proposal recently presented by the United States. We will continue championing a ceasefire, advocating for the release of all hostages and the access of all humanitarian aid necessary for the civilian population. Moreover, we appreciate the holding of the International Conference on the Two-State Solution that was held last week at this General Assembly. It was an invaluable demonstration of consensus, and it was an inspiring example of multilateral action. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Chile. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation.

Madam President, distinguished colleagues, nearly 2 weeks ago, On September 18th, the United States, for the 7th time since the escalation of the Palestinian-Israeli conflict on October 7th, 2023, used its veto to block a draft resolution prepared by the non-permanent members of the Security Council, a resolution focused on the humanitarian situation in the Gaza Strip. That document contained nothing that would not have found support among the overwhelming majority of of delegations gathered in this hall. It contained the demand for an immediate and unconditional ceasefire, the release of all hostages held by Hamas, the lifting of the humanitarian blockade of Gaza, and the provision of safe and unhindered access to those in need. Unfortunately, in Washington and in West Jerusalem, these fundamental humanitarian elements aimed at alleviating the suffering of the Palestinian people are stubbornly being interpreted as a reward to Hamas from the international community for the terrorist attack of October 7th. That same distorted logic is being applied to the recent wave of recognitions of Palestine by a number of Western states. It is difficult to understand how the international community is supposedly indulging Hamas when it demands the immediate and unconditional release of hostages, and when the New York Declaration clearly states that future control over Gaza should be transferred to the Palestinian National Authority. The Hamas attack on October 7th undoubtedly deserves condemnation, but it cannot be used to justify the collective punishment of innocent Palestinians or as a pretext to fuel war in the Middle East. In our view, the most recent veto was more of a gift to Israel, an undeserved reward for West Jerusalem's course of continuing military operations in Gaza, regardless of civilian casualties and the horrific humanitarian catastrophe in the Strip. Washington is thus attempting to reduce the role of the Security Council to that of a passive observer of the tragedy which is unfolding. Even the resolutions that were adopted over the past 2 years were either publicly declared non-legally binding like Resolution 2728, or remained on paper like Resolution 2735 with the infamous Biden plan. However, the Security Council must act. It must not content itself with the role assigned to it by the US and Israel. Our efforts must focus on the prospect of a two-state solution, which West Jerusalem is trying to cast aside at all costs. cost. We note that the situation in the occupied Palestinian territory and in the Middle East will be one of the key agenda items at the first Russia-League of Arab States summit, which will be held in Moscow on October 15th. We are convinced that the principled position of 14 out of 15 Security Council members and our collective efforts are bearing fruit. The Security Council's consideration of the draft resolution, as well as the recent high-level international conference to support the two-state solution have given momentum to the negotiation process around the Palestinian-Israeli conflict. In this context, serious attention should be given to the plan recently presented by U.S. President Donald Trump to end Israel's military operation in Gaza. That plan includes important elements such as a ceasefire, the withdrawal of Israeli troops from Gaza, release of hostages, hostages and detainees, scaling up humanitarian aid under UN auspices and as well as those of the Red Crescent, rejection of forced displacement of Gazans, and occupation or annexation of Gaza. We note that this initiative has been supported by leading countries of the Arab and Muslim world. The Palestinian National Authority is also ready to constructively engage with all partners develop a comprehensive peace agreement. Importantly, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has not opposed the plan. We are convinced that any steps and initiatives aimed at the immediate cessation of hostilities and bloodshed in Gaza deserve support. The next stage should be the launch of large-scale efforts to rebuild the infrastructure of the Strip, which lies in ruins due to the hostilities. We hope that the plan will receive sustained support from both sides and that its successful implementation will pave the way for the relaunching of the peace process on a universally recognized international legal basis centered around the two-state solution. There is no alternative to this. Moreover, during the 2 rounds of the High-Level International Conference on Palestine, a broad consensus was confirmed regarding the recognition of the legitimate rights and aspirations of of the Palestinian people to their own independent state within the 1967 borders, with its capital in East Jerusalem, coexisting in peace and security with Israel. This is a position that Russia has consistently and unwaveringly held for many years. Thank you for your attention.

Madam President, we recognize and value the leadership shown by the elected members of the Security Council of the United Nations.

When they championed and tabled draft resolution S/2025/583, we deeply regret the fact that that text, whose primary goal was to demand an immediate, unconditional, and permanent ceasefire in Gaza, as well as the release of all hostages still in Hamas hands, as well as Unfettered access of humanitarian aid. We deeply regret that it was vetoed by a permanent member of the Council on the 18th of September. Guatemala reaffirms its support for the Franco-Mexican initiative. That initiative seeks to suspend the veto when what is at stake is preventing or halting situations involving mass atrocities. As the United Nations, we have not discharged our mandate, that is, to act when military operators lay waste to individuals, families, or communities in their entirety in the name of security and sovereignty, particularly when what we're talking about are urgent decisions to save lives and to guarantee adherence to international humanitarian law. We have failed in that mission. Madam President, in Guatemala's view, a last peace in the region will not— will only be achieved if we apply a political solution and not a military one. Our solution must be based on the coexistence of 2 states, a solution which allows Israel and Palestine to live side by side in peace and security within defined, safe, and internationally recognized borders. This should guarantee the peaceful coexistence of the 2 peoples in accordance with the relevant resolutions of the Security Council and the United Nations General Assembly. As a founding member of this organization, Guatemala reaffirms its commitment to the fundamental principles of multilateralism. These principles must guide our collective efforts to preserve peace, protect human rights, and to guarantee the dignity The responsibility to protect, prevent, and respond to threats against peace is a responsibility that falls squarely on all of our shoulders, but particularly on those of the permanent members of the Security Council. I thank the distinguished representative of Guatemala, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Spain.

Madam President, Spain is grateful for the convening of this United Nations General Assembly special session following the Security Council's inability to adopt a resolution calling for an immediate and unconditional ceasefire on the 18th of September. That followed the veto being cast by one of its permanent members. We wish to thank the Security Council And particularly the 14 members of it that voted in favour of the resolution. We thank them for their efforts to agree upon a text to put an end to the violence in Gaza. As we stand just a few days away from marking 2 years since the beginning of the war, the Security Council's agreement was more necessary than ever. It may constitute a significant step forward. We appeal to the parties to commit to ending the violence. It is urgent that we halt the suffering that has gone on for too long. The war must end, and we must work to bring about a lasting peace on the basis of mutual of the implementation of the two-state solution. In this connection, the historic New York Declaration, supported by the vast majority of the international community, and the Peace Conference in New York for the implementation of the two-state solution confirmed that there is strong consensus within the international community around the need to implement the two-state solution that is seen as the only viable path towards a just and lasting peace. It is our roadmap to end the conflict. And in accordance with the New York Declaration, the Global Alliance for the Implementation of the Two-State Solution is the mechanism that will allow us to turn proposals into concrete actions. Spain has always been very clear as regards its position on the conflict. The ratcheting up of Israeli military operations on the city of Gaza The destruction of critical infrastructure such as hospitals or schools, the forced displacement of the Palestinian population, are flagrant violations of international law, of international humanitarian law, and of international human rights law. In the West Bank, we condemn the growing settler violence, the operations of the Israeli forces, and the policy of settlement expansion. Spain reiterates that settlements are illegal. Under international law. They are a threat to peace and they hinder the implementation of the two-state solution. The humanitarian situation in Gaza is marked by famine and is unconscionable. We will continue to demand the rapid and unfettered entry of humanitarian aid at scale.
